title: No thief of the will
hook: Marcus quotes Epictetus: no one can rob us of our will (Meditations 11.36)

segments.voice: Yesterday: remember a good person. Your line was remember them. Whose face did you call up, and when? Day six hundred twenty-seven.

Someone steals your bike. Someone takes credit for your idea. Someone cuts your hours, or your budget, or your part in the school play. Life has a lot of thieves. Toward the end of book eleven, Marcus stops writing his own thoughts for a while and copies out a string of sayings from Epictetus, the teacher who had once been enslaved. One of them is only a few words long, and it names the one thing no thief can take. Today: no thief of the will.
screen: `LIFE HAS A LOT OF THIEVES.` → `MARCUS COPIES EPICTETUS.` → `NO THIEF OF THE WILL.`

segments.voice: First, who's speaking. Epictetus was born into slavery, studied philosophy, and later taught it as a free man in Greece. As far as we know, Marcus never met him. But in book one Marcus thanks his teacher Rusticus for lending him Epictetus's discourses from his own library. Near the end of book eleven, Marcus writes out several Epictetus lines in a row, like favorite quotations copied into a notebook. Second, the line. A thief of the will, Marcus quotes, doesn't exist. No one can rob you of your choice. Third, the word. The Greek is prohairesis: the power to choose, to decide what you'll agree to, what you'll want, what you'll do. For Epictetus it's the one thing that truly belongs to you. Your body, your possessions, your reputation, your job can all be taken. Your choice about how to meet the loss can't be. Fourth, what it doesn't mean. It doesn't mean nothing hurts, or that circumstances don't matter. A person in prison has fewer choices than a person on a beach, and Epictetus knew that better than most. But even inside narrow walls, he taught, there's still the choice of how you stand there. That small, steady choice is what no one can steal.
screen: `EPICTETUS, ONCE ENSLAVED.` · `NO ONE CAN ROB YOUR CHOICE.` · `PROHAIRESIS: THE POWER TO CHOOSE.` · `EVEN INSIDE NARROW WALLS.` · then, large: `NO THIEF.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of something that's been taken from you, small or large: time, a plan, an opportunity, a person's trust. Let yourself feel the loss honestly. Then look for what wasn't taken: your choice about how to respond, right now. Pick one small choice you'll make about it today: a word, an action, an attitude. Hold it. Nobody handed it to you, and nobody can take it. That one is yours. The bell holds the time.
No thief of the will. Epictetus's line, copied by Marcus: no one can rob you of your choice. Today's word.
screen: `NO THIEF OF THE WILL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: no thief. When something is taken from you today, name the choice that's still yours, and make it. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Readers of Epictetus and Marcus often respond to a loss by naming what remains in their control, their response, and making one deliberate choice about it.

original.note: Greek: choice, will, the power to decide. Epictetus's word for what is truly ours.

trapdoor: what you thought: you can't control anything but yourself.
what it means: whatever is taken, the choice of how to meet it stays yours; no thief can reach it.
what a scholar hears: prohairesis is Epictetus's central term; Marcus came to Epictetus through Rusticus, who lent him the discourses.
